title: What the Wilderness Season Actually Produces in You (That Nothing Else Can)
fullText: Moses spent 40 years in the wilderness of Midian. 40 years, not 40 days, not 40 months, four decades of leading sheep through a desert, sleeping under open sky, far from everything he had known. He had been educated in the finest court in the ancient world, trained as a prince of Egypt, by some accounts, a candidate for the throne itself, and then in one moment, a body in the sand, a pharaoh who wanted him dead, everything was gone. He ran, and he kept running until he ended up in Midian, tending sheep that weren't even his own. Scripture is careful to note that detail. The sheep belonged to his father-in-law. The man who had been heir to the most powerful kingdom on earth was now watching someone else's livestock in the back of a desert for 40 years. And then one ordinary morning, just another morning, just another flock, just another stretch of rocky ground. He turned aside to look at a bush that was burning without being consumed. And God spoke to him from it. What came out of that wilderness was not the same man who had gone in. The man who stood before Pharaoh, who parted the Red Sea, who interceded for an entire nation when God was ready to destroy them, that man had been built in the desert. Not despite the desert, because of it. There are things the wilderness produces in you that no other season can, not the mountaintop, not the harvest, not the season of blessing and abundance, only the wilderness. And if you are in one right now, I want to tell you what God is building specifically in this season that he cannot build any other way. Before we go through what the wilderness produces, I need to make a distinction that matters enormously. The wilderness in the Bible is not one thing. It is at least two different things that look identical from the outside but are completely different on the inside. There is the wilderness of preparation. This is where Moses was, where Paul was, where Jesus was, where John the Baptist spent his entire early life. This wilderness is not accidental. It is appointed. The Spirit led Jesus into it, not around it, not through it quickly. Into it on purpose. And there is the wilderness of discipline, the one Israel inhabited for 40 years, circling the same ground, returning to the same failures. That wilderness extended itself, not because God had no destination for them, but because they refused to be changed by it. Numbers 14 records the moment the first generation sealed their own fate at Cadesh Bania. They stood at the border of the promised land, heard the report, and chose unbelief. God said 40 years, one year for each day the spies were in the land. The two wildernesses look almost exactly the same from the outside. Same heat, same silence, same sense of being lost. But inside, one is producing something, the other is circling. So before anything else, ask yourself honestly, am I growing in this wilderness or am I circling? Am I being formed or am I just waiting to be done? The answer to that question will tell you more about your wilderness than the circumstances of it. If you are being formed, if there is something building in your character, even as your circumstances remain difficult, then what follows is what God is building and it is worth every day of the desert. The first thing the wilderness produces is the death of self-reliance and nothing else kills it as completely. Moses at 40 years old was by any human measure qualified. He was educated in Egyptian science, literature, military strategy, and state craft. He was physically powerful. Acts 7:22 says he was powerful in speech and action. He had connections at the highest levels of the most powerful government in the world. And when he saw an Egyptian beating a Hebrew slave, he looked both ways, killed the Egyptian, and buried him in the sand. Confident, decisive, self-sufficient, that is not who emerged from 40 years in Midian. When God spoke to Moses from the burning bush and gave him the assignment to return to Egypt, Moses said, "Who am I that I should go to Pharaoh?" He said, "I have never been eloquent, neither in the past nor since you have spoken to your servant. I am slow of speech and tongue." He said, "Finally, pardon your servant, Lord. Please send someone else." The same man who had single-handedly taken the life of an Egyptian soldier now stood before God and said, "I cannot do this. Please send someone else." 40 years of watching sheep had done something to him, something irreversible. It had taken a man who believed in his own ability to fix things and turned him into a man who knew with total clarity that he could not. And that was exactly the man God needed. Because here is the theological truth underneath this. God does not add divine power on top of human self-sufficiency. He replaces human self-sufficiency with divine dependence. And those are very different operations. One stacks, the other empties before it fills. The wilderness is the emptying process. Gideon is a second witness to this. When the angel of the Lord found him, he was hiding inside a wine press, threshing wheat in secret so the Midionites wouldn't find him and take it. The angel called him mighty warrior. Gideon's response was immediate. My clan is the weakest in Manasseh and I am the least in my family. The self assessment was accurate. He was by every external measurement unremarkable. God said I will be with you. Not I will upgrade you. Not I will make you stronger. I will be with you. The presence of God as the resource not the improved version of Gideon. Self-reliance does not die comfortably. It dies in the wilderness. It dies in the absence of applause. In the absence of an audience, in the absence of the structures that gave you your identity. It dies when the sheep won't cooperate and there is no one watching. It dies slowly over years in the back of the desert. And when it is dead, when you have stood before God and said, "I cannot do this. Please send someone else. You are ready." Not because you became more capable, but because you finally became available for something that requires him and not just you. The diagnostic question here, has this wilderness killed something in you that needed to die? Is there a confidence you used to have in your own ability that the desert has quietly dismantled? If yes, don't mourn it. That is the first thing the wilderness had to produce, and it is producing it. The second thing the wilderness produces is an intimacy with God that cannot be manufactured anywhere else. Not in church, not in community, not in blessing. The pattern in scripture is consistent enough to be called a law. God speaks most clearly in the quietest places. He did not speak to Elijah in the earthquake, not in the fire, not in the great wind that tore the mountains apart. He spoke in a still small voice a sound so subtle that in some Hebrew translations it is rendered the sound of sheer silence after the earthquake after the fire in the stillness that followed. That is where the voice was. He did not give Moses the Torah on a busy city street. He gave it on a mountain in the wilderness in 40 days of solitude and silence. He did not reveal the depth of the gospel to Paul in Jerusalem surrounded by other apostles who could have informed him. Paul writes in Galatians 1 that after his Damascus road conversion, he did not go up to Jerusalem. He went into Arabia 3 years. What he was doing there, scripture does not fully say. But what he came back with a gospel so complete, so theologically precise, so independent of any human source that he could write to the Galatians, I did not receive it from any man, nor was I taught it. But I received it through a revelation of Jesus Christ that came from somewhere quiet, from somewhere alone. And then there is Jesus himself. 30 years of obscurity in Nazareth before 3 years of public ministry. And even during those three years, scripture shows him repeatedly withdrawing. Before choosing the 12, after feeding the 5,000, before the hardest days, after the most public victories, he withdrew to pray alone. The son of God in whom the fullness of the deity dwelled bodily, and he still needed the quiet place. He still needed the alone place. He still chose the wilderness. What does this tell us? that the intimacy the wilderness produces is not the byproduct of having nothing else to do. It is the product of a specific kind of attention that only becomes possible when the noise is gone. The wilderness strips away the voices, the distractions, the communities, the structures, everything you might mistake for God's voice until what remains is only God's voice. And when you have heard God in the wilderness, when you have had the experience of his presence, not in a crowd or in a moment of blessing, but in a hard, quiet, stripped down place with nothing else, you know something about him that cannot be transmitted by any other method. You know him from the inside. You have heard the still small voice. You know what it sounds like. Moses at the burning bush was alone. He had led the flock to the back of the desert, scripture says the remote side, the furthest point from people. And it was there, in the most obscure corner of an obscure wilderness, that God revealed his name. I am who I am. The most profound self-disclosure in all of the Old Testament happened in a place no one else would have gone. The question for you in this wilderness, are you treating the silence as a void to be filled with content, with plans, with noise of any kind, or as an invitation? What if the quiet is not the absence of God, but the precise environment in which he is most clearly heard? The third thing the wilderness produces is endurance. And here is the thing about endurance. It cannot be given. It can only be built and it is built through sustained exposure to difficulty, not through relief from it. James 1:3 says, "The testing of your faith produces steadfastness." Not suggests, not might produce, produces. It is a manufacturing statement. This is what the testing process makes. And steadfastness, when it reaches its full effect, produces something that is perfect and complete. lacking in nothing. Perfect and complete, lacking in nothing. That is the end product of endurance. Not comfort, not convenience, completeness. But the manufacturing process cannot be bypassed. You cannot receive the product without the process. There is no shortcut to endurance because endurance is by definition the capacity to keep going when you want to stop. And that capacity only develops through the experience of wanting to stop and choosing to keep going anyway. This is why the wilderness of Israel and the wilderness of Moses were the same geography but produced completely different outcomes. Israel wanted out. From the moment things got difficult, they wanted to go back to Egypt. They romanticized their slavery. At least in Egypt, we had meat and bread, they said, while mana fell from the sky every morning. They could not endure the discomfort of the process because they had not chosen to be formed by it. Moses tending sheep for 40 years was being given something Israel kept refusing. Every morning with the flock was a day of endurance that no one was watching. No crowd, no applause, no visible progress toward anything significant. Just faithfulness in the daily unremarkable work of keeping sheep alive. And then when God called him to lead 2 million people through that same desert for another 40 years, Moses had already been in the wilderness longer than the journey would take. He had been formed for exactly this. His endurance was not self-produced. It had been built by sustained exposure to the very environment he would need to lead others through. Paul understood this from the inside. He writes in Romans 5 that suffering produces endurance and endurance produces character and character produces hope. That is a manufacturing chain. Each product in the chain is produced by the thing that came before it. You cannot get to hope by skipping the suffering. You cannot get to character by skipping the endurance. The chain is linear. The process is sequential. The wilderness is where the first link in that chain is being formed. The fourth thing the wilderness produces is perhaps the most unexpected authority. A particular kind of authority that can only come from having been through something. There is a difference between someone who teaches about suffering and someone who has suffered. between someone who talks about trusting God in the dark and someone who did it in the dark for years with no visible result. The difference is not just credibility. It is weight. One voice carries an authority the other cannot manufacture. John the Baptist spent his life in the wilderness. Luke 1:80 says that he grew and became strong in spirit and he was in the deserts until the day of his public appearance to Israel. his entire childhood and young adulthood in the wilderness. Living on locusts and wild honey, wearing camels hair, not building a network, not acquiring credentials, just the desert year after year. And then he emerged. And when he spoke, something happened that rarely happened in Israel. The people came not to a city, not to a temple, to the wilderness, to a river. Crowds left Jerusalem and all Judea and went to the Jordan to peer this man. Matthew 3:5 says, "Jerusalem and all Judea and all the region about the Jordan were going out to him." The wilderness had produced something in his voice that drew people out of cities. Moses when he stood before Pharaoh spoke with the quiet authority of a man who had been emptied of his own ambition for 40 years. He was not trying to prove himself. He was not performing. He was delivering a message that was not his own on behalf of a god who had appeared to him in a burning bush in the back of the desert. The authority in his voice was not his, but it was real. And Pharaoh, one of the most powerful men alive, felt it. Jesus, when he emerged from 40 days in the wilderness and began teaching, the crowds were astonished because he taught them as one who had authority and not as their scribes. The wilderness had done something that three decades of synagogue attendance could not produce. The scribes knew the same texts, but they did not have the weight of the wilderness in their voices. Here is what this means for you. The wilderness you are in right now is not only forming your character. It is forming your voice. The things you will one day say to someone sitting in their own desert. The words that will reach them in ways that polished theology cannot. Those words are being forged right now. In this silence, in this difficulty, in this season when nothing seems to be happening, you are earning a kind of authority that cannot be purchased, taught, or inherited. It can only be lived. One thing needs to be said before we close. The wilderness produces these things only when you let it. The same desert that built Moses for 40 years extended Israel's journey for 40 more because they refused to be changed by it. The wilderness is not passive. It makes an offer. The offer is be formed here. Learn what I am teaching here. Let what is not true about you die here. Let what is true about God deepen here. You can refuse the offer. You can spend the entire wilderness season anesthetizing yourself from it, filling the silence, avoiding the solitude, demanding explanation, romanticizing the Egypt you came from. And the wilderness will remain a wilderness. No product, no formation, just time passing in a hard place. The people who emerge from the wilderness carrying something are the people who stopped fighting the wilderness and started asking what it was trying to build. So, if you are in a wilderness right now, here are the questions that come out of everything we just walked through. What is the self-reliance this season is trying to kill? What is the ability, the identity, the confidence in your own strength that the desert is quietly dismantling? Let it go. What God puts in its place will be worth it. Is the silence in this wilderness an invitation you've been treating as a void? What would change if you stopped trying to fill it and started listening in it? What is being built in your endurance right now that cannot be built any other way? What link in the chain is being forged in this difficulty that will hold weight later? And who are you becoming in this wilderness? Because the voice you will carry out of this season, the authority, the weight, the credibility of someone who has been through something real that is being shaped right now. Every day you stay faithful in the back of the desert is a day that voice becomes more real. Moses led the flock to the back of the desert on the morning he encountered the burning bush. Not toward the city, not toward people, to the furthest, most obscure corner of the wilderness. It was there in the place no one else would have gone on an ordinary morning indistinguishable from 40 years of ordinary mornings that the bush caught his attention. Scripture says he turned aside to see. That phrase matters. He could have kept walking. He could have written it off. He had been in this desert long enough that a burning bush might have seemed like one more strange thing in a strange place. But he turned aside. And when God saw that he had turned aside to look, he called to him from the bush. The encounter was waiting on the willingness to stop and pay attention to what the wilderness was showing him. Everything. Moses became the deliverer, the lawgiver, the intercessor, the man of God began in that moment. But that moment required 40 years to produce a man who had been emptied enough, quieted enough, formed enough to turn aside and hear. The wilderness is not the pause between your story and the story that matters. The wilderness is where the person is being built who can live the story that matters. Turn aside. Pay attention to what is burning in your desert.
fullTextVi: Môi-se sống 40 năm trong hoang mạc Ma-đi-an. 40 năm, không phải 40 ngày, không phải 40 tháng, bốn thập kỷ dẫn dắt đàn cừu một sa mạc, ngủ yên dưới bầu trời rộng mở, cách xa mọi thứ anh từng biết. Anh ta đã được giáo dục trong triều đình tốt nhất thế giới cổ đại, được đào tạo thành một hoàng tử của Ai Cập, theo một số tài khoản, là một ứng cử viên cho ngai vàng và rồi trong một khoảnh khắc, một cơ thể trên cát, một pharaoh muốn anh ta chết rồi, mọi thứ đều biến mất. Anh ta chạy, và cứ chạy cho đến khi đến Midian, chăn cừu đó thậm chí không phải của riêng anh ấy. Kinh thánh cẩn thận lưu ý chi tiết đó. Con cừu thuộc về bố vợ anh. Người đàn ông từng là người thừa kế vương quốc hùng mạnh nhất trên trái đất là hiện đang theo dõi gia súc của người khác ở phía sau sa mạc trong 40 năm. Và rồi một buổi sáng bình thường, chỉ một buổi sáng khác, chỉ một đàn khác, chỉ một đoạn đường khác của đất đá. Ông quay lại nhìn một bụi cây đang cháy nhưng không tàn. Và Chúa đã phán với ông từ đó. Người bước ra từ vùng hoang dã đó không phải là người đàn ông đã đi in. Người đứng trước mặt Pharaoh, người đã chia cắt Biển Đỏ, người cầu thay cho cả một quốc gia khi Chúa sẵn sàng tiêu diệt họ, người đàn ông đó đã được xây dựng trên sa mạc. Không phải bất chấp sa mạc, vì nó. Có những điều mà vùng hoang dã tạo ra trong bạn mà không mùa nào khác có thể làm được, không đỉnh núi, không phải mùa màng, không phải mùa phúc lộc trù phú, chỉ có hoang mạc. Và nếu bạn đang ở trong một trong số đó ngay bây giờ, tôi muốn nói với bạn điều gì Chúa đang xây dựng đặc biệt trong thời điểm này mà Ngài không thể xây dựng theo cách nào khác. Trước khi chúng ta xem qua những gì vùng hoang dã tạo ra, tôi cần phân biệt điều đó rất quan trọng. Đồng vắng trong Kinh thánh không phải là một chuyện. Đó là ít nhất hai thứ khác nhau trông giống hệt nhau từ bên ngoài nhưng bên trong hoàn toàn khác nhau. Có sự hoang dã của sự chuẩn bị. Đây là nơi Moses đã ở, nơi Paul ở, nơi Chúa Giêsu ở, nơi John the Baptist đã dành toàn bộ cuộc đời đầu tiên của mình. Sự hoang dã này không phải là ngẫu nhiên. Nó được bổ nhiệm. Thánh Linh đã dẫn dắt Chúa Giêsu vào trong đó, không phải đi vòng quanh, không xuyên qua nó một cách nhanh chóng. Vào nó có mục đích. Và có đồng vắng kỷ luật, nơi dân Y-sơ-ra-ên đã ở trong 40 năm, đi vòng quanh cùng một mặt đất, quay lại với những thất bại tương tự. Vùng hoang dã đó tự mở rộng, không phải vì Chúa không có đích đến cho họ, mà vì họ từ chối bị nó thay đổi. Số 14 ghi lại khoảnh khắc thế hệ đầu tiên tự phong ấn số phận của mình tại Cadesh Bania. Họ đứng ở biên giới đất hứa, nghe báo cáo và chọn sự không tin. Chúa phán 40 năm, một năm cho mỗi ngày các điệp viên ở trong land. Hai vùng hoang dã trông gần như giống hệt nhau từ bên ngoài. Cùng hơi ấm, cùng sự im lặng, cùng cảm giác lạc lõng. Nhưng bên trong, một cái đang sản xuất thứ gì đó, cái kia đang quay vòng. Vì vậy, trước bất cứ điều gì khác, hãy thành thật tự hỏi bản thân, liệu tôi đang lớn lên ở nơi hoang dã này hay tôi đang đi vòng à? Tôi đang được hình thành hay tôi chỉ đang chờ đợi để được hoàn thành? Câu trả lời cho câu hỏi đó sẽ cho bạn biết nhiều hơn về vùng hoang dã của bạn hơn hoàn cảnh của nó. Nếu bạn đang được hình thành, nếu có điều gì đó hình thành trong tính cách của bạn, thậm chí vì hoàn cảnh của các bạn vẫn còn khó khăn, nên điều tiếp theo là những gì Chúa đang xây dựng và nó có giá trị mỗi ngày của sa mạc. Điều đầu tiên mà vùng hoang dã tạo ra là cái chết của sự tự lực và không có gì khác giết chết nó hoàn toàn. Ở tuổi 40, Môi-se đã đủ tiêu chuẩn theo bất kỳ tiêu chuẩn nào của con người. Ông được đào tạo về khoa học, văn học, chiến lược quân sự và thủ công nhà nước của Ai Cập. Anh ấy có sức mạnh thể chất. Công vụ 7:22 nói rằng ông có quyền năng trong lời nói và hành động. Anh ta có mối quan hệ ở cấp cao nhất của chính phủ quyền lực nhất trong thế giới. Và khi nhìn thấy một người Ai Cập đánh đập một nô lệ người Do Thái, anh ta nhìn cả hai phía, giết người Ai Cập và chôn hắn trong cát. Tự tin, quyết đoán, tự chủ, đó không phải là người đã nổi lên từ 40 năm ở Midian. Khi Chúa phán với Môi-se từ bụi gai cháy và giao cho ông nhiệm vụ để trở về Ai Cập, Moses nói, "Tôi là ai mà tôi nên đến gặp Pharaoh? " Anh ta nói, "Tôi chưa bao giờ là người có tài hùng biện, cả trong quá khứ lẫn kể từ đó ngài đã nói chuyện với người hầu của mình. Tôi chậm nói và lưỡi. " Anh ta nói: "Cuối cùng, xin hãy tha thứ cho người hầu của ngài, thưa Chúa. Xin hãy cử người khác đi. " Cũng chính là người đã một mình lấy đi mạng sống của một người lính Ai Cập bây giờ đứng trước Chúa và nói: "Tôi không thể làm điều này. Xin vui lòng gửi người khác. " 40 năm chăn cừu đã làm một điều gì đó với anh ta, một điều không thể thay đổi được. Nó đã biến một người đàn ông tin vào khả năng sửa chữa mọi thứ của chính mình và biến anh ta thành một người hoàn toàn hiểu rõ rằng mình có thể not. Và đó chính xác là người mà Chúa cần. Bởi vì đây là lẽ thật thần học bên dưới điều này. Thiên Chúa không thêm sức mạnh thần thánh vào khả năng tự túc của con người. Ngài thay thế sự tự túc của con người bằng sự phụ thuộc vào thần thánh. Và đó là những hoạt động rất khác nhau. Một ngăn xếp, cái còn lại trống trước khi nó đầy. Hoang dã là quá trình làm trống rỗng. Gideon là nhân chứng thứ hai cho việc này. Khi thiên thần của Chúa tìm thấy anh ta, anh ta đang trốn trong rượu nhấn, bí mật đập lúa mì để người Midionites không tìm thấy anh ta và lấy đi. Thiên thần gọi anh là chiến binh dũng mãnh. Phản ứng của Gideon là ngay lập tức. Gia tộc của tôi yếu nhất ở Manasseh và tôi là người kém nhất trong gia đình. Tự đánh giá là chính xác. Theo mọi phép đo bên ngoài, anh ấy không có gì nổi bật. Chúa nói tôi sẽ ở bên bạn. Không phải tôi sẽ nâng cấp cho bạn. Không phải tôi sẽ làm cho bạn mạnh mẽ hơn. Tôi sẽ ở bên bạn. Sự hiện diện của Chúa là nguồn tài nguyên chứ không phải phiên bản cải tiến của Gideon. Tự lực không chết thoải mái. Nó chết ở nơi hoang dã. Nó chết khi không có tiếng vỗ tay. Trong trường hợp không có khán giả, không có các cấu trúc mang lại danh tính của bạn. Nó chết khi đàn cừu không hợp tác và không có ai trông chừng. Nó chết dần dần qua nhiều năm ở phía sau sa mạc.
